title: Analysing and stress-testing results
summary: Get results out the same way every time, compare against Reference, decompose changes in transport CO2, stress-test with sensitivity runs and scenario discovery, and benchmark against other models.
outcomes: Extract transport results with saved queries into tidy tables
Report every policy result as a difference from Reference
Decompose a change in transport CO2 into activity, structure, intensity and carbon effects
Stress-test findings with a tornado chart and scenario discovery, and benchmark against AR6
narration_en: A result is only as good as the way you get it out and test it. Step one: use the same saved queries every time, and save tidy tables, so that every figure can be rebuilt. Step two: never report a policy run alone. Report the difference from the Reference run, and explain it. Step three: decompose the change. The logarithmic mean Divisia index splits a change in transport carbon dioxide into four parts that add up exactly: more travel, a shift between modes, less energy per passenger-kilometre, and less carbon per unit of energy. Step four: stress-test. A tornado chart shows which single assumption moves the result most. An ensemble with scenario discovery finds the combinations of inputs that lead to high emissions. In the course kit's toy ensemble, the battery electric vehicle cost explained most high-emission runs, followed by the carbon price. Step five: benchmark against other models, for example the IPCC's AR6 scenario database, and explain any differences.
narration_ar: النتيجة لا تكون أفضل من الطريقة التي تستخرجها بها وتختبرها. الخطوة الأولى: استخدم الاستعلامات المحفوظة نفسها في كل مرة، واحفظ جداول مرتبة، حتى يمكن إعادة بناء كل شكل. الخطوة الثانية: لا تعرض نتيجة سيناريو السياسة وحدها أبدًا، بل اعرض الفرق عن سيناريو الأساس وفسّره. الخطوة الثالثة: فكّك التغيير. فمؤشر ديفيزيا للمتوسط اللوغاريتمي يقسم التغير في انبعاثات ثاني أكسيد الكربون من النقل إلى أربعة أجزاء مجموعها مساوٍ للتغير تمامًا: زيادة السفر، والتحول بين الوسائل، وانخفاض الطاقة لكل راكب-كيلومتر، وانخفاض الكربون لكل وحدة طاقة. الخطوة الرابعة: اختبر متانة النتائج. فمخطط الإعصار يبيّن أي افتراض منفرد يحرّك النتيجة أكثر من غيره. ومجموعة التشغيلات مع اكتشاف السيناريوهات تجد تركيبات المدخلات التي تؤدي إلى انبعاثات مرتفعة. وفي مجموعة التشغيلات التجريبية في حقيبة المقرر، فسّرت تكلفة السيارة الكهربائية بالبطاريات معظم التشغيلات عالية الانبعاثات، يليها سعر الكربون. الخطوة الخامسة: قارن نتائجك بالنماذج الأخرى، مثل قاعدة بيانات سيناريوهات التقرير السادس للهيئة الحكومية الدولية المعنية بتغير المناخ، وفسّر أي اختلافات.

tour.text: Extract results with saved queries into tidy tables, the same way every time.
Report each policy as its difference from Reference.
Decompose the change to explain it: activity, structure, intensity, carbon.
Stress-test: rank single assumptions, then search an ensemble for what drives bad outcomes.
Benchmark against other models; keep only findings that survive.

sections.heading: Step 1: get the numbers out, the same way every time
sections.html:
Write one script that runs every query you need for every scenario and saves one tidy table (scenario, region, year, variable, item, value, unit). Never copy numbers from ModelInterface by hand. The transport queries live in output/queries/Main_queries.xml; the kit's query file collects the ones a transport study needs.

sections.heading: Step 2: compare against Reference, then explain
sections.html:
The policy effect is the difference between two runs that share everything else. Report absolute differences (Mt) and relative ones (% of Reference), per capita where regions differ in size, and cumulatively where the climate is concerned.

sections.heading: Step 3: decompose the change
sections.html:
To explain why transport CO2 differs between two years or two scenarios, split it into factors, exactly like the Kaya identity in Go 1 but for transport. For each mode m:

CO2 = Σm A · Sm · Im · Fm(3.8)

with A total activity (pkm), Sm the mode share, Im energy per pkm and Fm CO2 per unit of energy. The logarithmic mean Divisia index (LMDI) attributes the change to each factor with no leftover residual:

ΔCO2(X) = Σm L(Cm1, Cm0) · ln(Xm1 ⁄ Xm0),    L(a, b) = (a − b) ⁄ (ln a − ln b)(3.9)

sections.heading: Step 4: stress-test
sections.html:
One at a time: the tornado

Move each uncertain input from its low to its high value with everything else central, and plot the range of the output. The longest bar is the input your conclusion depends on most. It is cheap (two runs per input) but misses interactions.

Input (low / high)BEV share at lowat highrange
BEV cost ±30%0.080.920.84
BEV share-weight 0.25 / 1.50.140.500.36
carbon price 0 / 200 $/t0.400.540.13
logit exponent −4 / −120.450.360.09

Many at once: ensembles and scenario discovery

Run a full factorial or Latin-hypercube ensemble in batch mode. Label each run "high" or "not high" for the outcome you care about (for example, 2050 transport CO2 above a target). Then search for a simple box in input space that captures the high runs — with the PRIM algorithm or a classification tree (lab 13 uses rpart). Judge the box with two numbers:

coverage = (high runs inside the box) ⁄ (all high runs),    density = (high runs inside the box) ⁄ (all runs inside the box)(3.10)

Read the output like this: the tree splits first on BEV cost, and the PRIM-style box keeps 80 % of the high runs with 92 % of runs inside it high (against a base rate of 25 %). The car load factor and GDP growth were never used — in this synthetic ensemble, they do not explain failure. With real GCAM runs, check that the box is stable when you re-sample.

sections.heading: Step 5: benchmark against other models
sections.html: Put your Reference and policy runs next to the AR6 scenario database (or the newer CMIP7 ScenarioMIP set) for the same region and variables: Final Energy|Transportation, Emissions|CO2|Energy|Demand|Transportation, Energy Service|Transportation|Passenger. Lab 12 shows how to filter AR6 runs to a similar carbon price. Being outside the range is not wrong, but you must be able to say why (module 3.3).

callouts.title: Why this matters
callouts.html: In the kit's toy transport model, filling cars with more people (the LF-up scenario) should cut emissions. By 2050 it cuts them by only 3 Mt out of 84 — because cheaper car travel makes people travel 15 % more and pulls them out of buses. The first number you look at is rarely the answer; the analysis is in explaining it.

callouts.title: Research note
callouts.html: Two toy artefacts worth noticing. (1) In the toy Reference, the BEV share jumps to about half of car pkm in 2030, because the share-weight switches from 0 to 1 between 2025 and 2030 and the toy has no vintages. GCAM smooths this with an s-curve and capital stock. (2) Sales-like shares ("tech (new)") move much faster than the stock of vehicles on the road (Figure 3.15 in module 3.7). Always say which one you report.

callouts.title: Worked calculation
callouts.html:
LMDI for an illustrative country (three modes, two years)

  1. CO2 falls from 19.36 to 13.13 Mt: a change of -6.24 Mt.
  2. Activity (pkm 200 → 300 bn): +6.49 Mt.
  3. Mode structure (cars 80 % → 70 %, rail 5 % → 15 %): -1.72 Mt.
  4. Energy intensity (cars 1.6 → 1.1 MJ/pkm, etc.): -5.71 Mt.
  5. Carbon intensity (fuel switching, cleaner electricity): -5.30 Mt.
  6. Sum of effects: -6.24 Mt — equal to the total change, with no residual.

Answer: intensity and carbon each cut more than mode shift; activity growth eats most of the gains

callouts.title: Worked calculation
callouts.html:
Scenario discovery on 36 runs

  1. 9 of the 36 runs miss the 2050 target ("high").
  2. Candidate box: "BEV cost high AND share-weight path slow" contains 10 runs, of which 7 are high.
  3. Coverage = 7 ÷ 9 = 0.78: the box explains 78 % of the failures.
  4. Density = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.70: inside the box, 70 % of runs fail.
  5. A good box has both high; narrowing the box raises density but lowers coverage — report the trade-off.

Answer: coverage 0.78, density 0.70

callouts.title: Pitfall
callouts.html: Reporting a percentage of the wrong base. "Transport CO2 falls 60 %" — below what? The 2020 level, or the 2050 Reference? The two can differ by a factor of two when Reference emissions grow. Always say "relative to Reference in the same year" or "relative to 2020".

callouts.title: Try it
callouts.html:
1. Using Eq. 3.9, what sign does the activity effect have if pkm stays constant? What if pkm falls?
  2. Your tree's best box has coverage 0.9 and density 0.3. Is it a useful finding? What would you try next?
  3. In Figure 3.11, which bar would you test first in a full GCAM ensemble, and why?

takeaways: Same queries, tidy tables, scripted figures: every number rebuildable
Report policy minus Reference, never a policy run alone
LMDI splits a CO2 change into activity, structure, intensity and carbon effects that add up exactly
Tornado charts rank single assumptions; scenario discovery finds combinations that matter
Benchmark against AR6 and other models, and explain the differences

code.title: LMDI decomposition, two modes
code.source:
# LMDI-I decomposition of a change in transport CO2 (two modes, illustrative numbers)
import numpy as np

def L(a, b):                       # logarithmic mean
    return a if abs(a - b) < 1e-12 else (a - b) / np.log(a / b)

A0, A1 = 1000.0, 1400.0            # passenger-km (billion)
S0, S1 = np.array([0.6, 0.4]), np.array([0.65, 0.35])   # mode shares: car, bus
I0, I1 = np.array([2.0, 0.6]), np.array([1.4, 0.42])    # MJ per pkm
F0, F1 = np.array([0.07, 0.07]), np.array([0.042, 0.042])  # kg CO2 per MJ

C0 = A0 * S0 * I0 * F0             # Mt CO2 by mode
C1 = A1 * S1 * I1 * F1
w = np.array([L(C1[i], C0[i]) for i in range(2)])
effects = {
    "activity":  float((w * np.log(A1 / A0)).sum()),
    "structure": float((w * np.log(S1 / S0)).sum()),
    "intensity": float((w * np.log(I1 / I0)).sum()),
    "carbon":    float((w * np.log(F1 / F0)).sum()),
}
for k, v in effects.items():
    print(f"{k:9s} {v:+8.2f} Mt")
print(f"sum of effects {sum(effects.values()):+.2f} Mt; actual change {C1.sum() - C0.sum():+.2f} Mt")
code.explain: The four effects use the logarithmic mean of start and end emissions for each mode, so they add up exactly to the total change. Try changing the shares or intensities.
